lines.narration: Sean goes where Han goes now, and that means standing at the back of a mahjong room while the men who own the night play tiles.

Morimoto, DK's wingman, asks when the next race is. That is not a question, that is bait. Han takes it: why not be in it. And the smile that cracks Sean's flat face is the first thing in Tokyo he has actually wanted.
Terms in nine seconds. Morimoto takes Han's 86 Corolla if Sean loses; Han puts up a 72 Skyline against it. Neither of them asks Sean whether he can drive.
Done, Morimoto says. Then the table is finished with Sean. Get him out of here.

What the table actually wants to know is where a shipment has gone. Han tells them to sit pretty and let him handle it, and he grins while he says it. Then the grin goes and his eyes drop. Everything that kills people later is wired to the thing Han just smiled his way past.

claim.subject: the long-haired man in the dark jacket

lines.narration: Out on the neon street he feeds a payphone and tells his father that school kept him late for extracurricular activities. He needs the night free. The lie buys it.

claim.subject: the American in the white shirt

lines.narration: He tells Neela she really needs to stop following him around. She says she only stopped by to ask his boyfriend for drifting lessons. He kills it dead: she does not want to be part of this world.

claim.subject: the woman in the fur-collar coat

lines.narration: She tells him he knows nothing about her, then proves she knows everything about him. Army brat. A new school every year, and a mother and a father who were never home.
The part that lands is the last of it: he walks around angry all the time, and he has swapped his family for a crowd of drift nuts. Zero for one, cowboy, he says, and neither of them believes it.
Driving out of the lantern-lit lane, Sean asks whether everything is okay back there. Han says he can handle it. That is twice.

Then Han lays out the actual shape of Tokyo. DK is Yakuza. His uncle Kamata takes a piece of everything on his turf, which is why nobody on these streets ever meets a policeman they cannot drive away from. Fifty percent of something beats a hundred percent of nothing, Han says, cheerful as weather.

Sean asks what the point of racing DK even is. Han pushes back: beating somebody only proves you are faster, so it has to be for something that matters. It is a strange creed from a man running on other people's money, and the film does not step in to defend him.
So why let him race at all? DK's pride is his kryptonite, Han says. Also, Sean still owes him a car.
The needle hits a hundred and ninety-seven kilometres an hour and a patrol car slots in behind them. Sean's grin falls off his face. In Arizona this cost him his third strike.

Han does not even sit up. These cars are factory tuned and top out at a hundred and eighty, he says, so above that the police do not bother. Sean argues, loses, and announces that he is beginning to like this country.
They pull in at Han's garage, which turns out to have a party bolted onto it. Watch how the room treats each of them.

Han moves through it like a mayor, a hand here, a name there, the room lighting up at the sight of him, while Sean trails two steps behind, carrying nothing, known by nobody. In Arizona he was the dangerous one. Here he is furniture.

Twinkie, his one friend at school, hooks an arm round his neck and explains the economics of the room: these women have been posing all day, they know nobody in town, and every man here is too scared to speak to them. So you talk to the little dude who makes you laugh.
Then he walks past a red Evo, and walks back to it.

Han gives it to him. Not lends. Sean represents him now, and Han is not letting his own name roll around Tokyo in a Hyundai. Generosity and branding in one sentence, and Han never does separate the two.
The first thing Sean does with the gift is take it to a dockside lot and try to destroy it.
On the sofas the crew are laughing. Sean has a race coming against the best drifter in Tokyo, and he still cannot drift. He keeps going anyway.
Morning. School blazer. Boswell in a neighbourhood garage with his hands deep in a stripped vintage coupe.

Then Boswell offers him a proverb he has clearly been saving: deru kui wa utarero. The nail that sticks out gets hammered. It is good advice and it is completely useless, because Sean has never once managed to be the nail that lies flat.

claim.subject: the grey-haired man in the grey henley

lines.narration: On the school roof, Twinkie is down on his hands and knees, and the blond classmate standing over him is playing it up for a laughing crew. Nobody in that ring will stop it.

Sean breaks into the circle with a hand up and calls it a misunderstanding, which is generous for a kid who sells knock-offs and does not do refunds. Nobody asked him to do this. He does it because standing at the back of a crowd is the one thing he has never managed.

claim.subject: the young American in the school blazer

lines.narration: Neela stays behind on the emptied roof. Not easy, saving the day, is it, she says, and then tells him he is doing all right. First approval anybody in this city has handed him for free.

She apologises for prying into his family. He tells her it is okay. Two people handed somebody else's country, feeling for the edges of each other, carefully, because the thing standing between them has a nickname and an uncle.
